::: {.callout-note}
Preliminary. One annotator tagged the cells by eye, and some calls were borderline.
All cells come from 8 confocal stacks, so they are not independent samples (see [Caveats](#caveats)).
Figures and tables are produced by `local-analysis/preliminary_report.py` from `data/aggregate/` and the tags.
:::

## Segmentation

Each stack has two channels: channel 0 shows nuclei and channel 1 shows the Texas red dye filling the
lacuno-canalicular network. Stacks are resampled to cubic voxels of 0.45–0.48 µm. The steps are:

1. **Seeds.** Cleaned channel-0 nuclei seed one region each. Very large channel-0 components are soft tissue, not nuclei.
2. **Soft tissue.** Channel 1 is thresholded and eroded so that osteocytes detach from the soft tissue. Eroded
   components that are too large are labelled soft tissue and become a competing seed.
3. **Watershed.** A seeded watershed runs on the channel-1 foreground, splitting the dye signal between the cells.
4. **Filters.** The following regions are removed:
   - regions near the edge of the bone, judged by distance from the in-plane convex hull of the cells;
   - regions lying beyond the soft tissue;
   - regions without a nucleus (regions holding several nuclei are split at them);
   - in some stacks, sheet-like regions.

Thresholds were tuned per stack because the dye intensity varies. Each stack's parameters are in its
`summary.json`, and its 3D scene and gallery are on its [series page](index.qmd#series).

## Dendrites

Let $M$ be a cell's voxel mask. The **body** $B$ is the morphological opening of $M$ by a ball of radius
$r = 2$ voxels, which removes everything thinner than about $2r + 1 \approx 2.4$ µm. Let $d_B(\mathbf{x})$ be the
distance of voxel $\mathbf{x}$ from $B$. Each connected component $P$ of $M \cap \{d_B > r\}$ is a
**protrusion**, with

$$
\text{reach}(P) = \max_{\mathbf{x} \in P} d_B(\mathbf{x}).
$$

A protrusion counts as a **dendrite** when two conditions hold:

- its reach is at least 2 µm (shorter ones are surface roughness);
- it is thin in two directions, i.e. not a sheet.

To test thinness, let $\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \lambda_3$ be the eigenvalues of the covariance of the
protrusion's voxel coordinates. A protrusion with linearity $\sqrt{\lambda_2/\lambda_1} \ge 0.65$ and planarity
$\sqrt{\lambda_3/\lambda_2} \le 0.25$ is broad and flat. Such a protrusion is a thin rim of the flattened cell body,
which the opening strips because it tests thickness only. It is assigned to the body and not counted.

The *cell body* used below is the cell minus its counted dendrites. Each cell's dialog on its series page has a
rotating image of this classification.

## Manual tagging

Every segmented cell was tagged by eye in a dedicated browser app (`local-analysis/annotate.py`). The app shows
a rotating 3D projection of the dye signal and orthogonal maximum projections. Cells come in a fixed random order
with no stack, label or measurement shown, so the tagging is blind to the numbers. The tags are:

- **elongated**;
- **round**;
- **blob/outlier**;
- **unsure**.

Blob/outlier and unsure cells were reviewed a second time and judged **junk**, **real but dirty**, **real (clean)**
or **unsure**. Junk cells are dropped from everything. Real cells that still have no type are kept in the counts
but left out of the two-group comparison.

{{< include preliminary/_counts.md >}}

: Cells per stack. {#tbl-counts}

Stacks 3.1 and 3.2 contain almost no round cells. All the group tests below therefore compare cells *within* each
stack, so differences between stacks cannot pass for differences between the groups.

## Metrics

Take the voxel coordinates of a region, in µm, with covariance eigenvalues $\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \lambda_3$.
Its axes are the full axes of the solid ellipsoid with the same second moments:

$$
a_k = 2\sqrt{5\lambda_k}, \qquad a_1 \ge a_2 \ge a_3 .
$$

| metric | definition |
|:--|:--|
| body length, width, thickness $a_1, a_2, a_3$ | axes of the cell body (dendrites removed) |
| body volume $V_b$, cell volume $V$ | voxel count × voxel volume, without / with the dendrites |
| cell axis ratio $a_2/a_1$ | axes of the whole cell; 0 = needle, 1 = round in its widest plane |
| body axis ratios $a_2/a_1$, $a_3/a_2$ | the same for the body; $a_3/a_2$ low = flattened |
| solidity $S$ | $V / V_{\text{convex hull}}$ |
| dendrites per cell $N_d$ | counted protrusions (see [Dendrites](#dendrites)) |
| dendrite reach | mean and maximum of $\text{reach}(P)$ over the cell's dendrites |
| total dendrite path | summed length of the dendrites' pruned skeletons beyond the body |
| process fraction $f_p$ | $1 - V_b / V$ |
| dendrite starriness $s$ | $1 - (t_1 - t_2)$, see below |
| nucleus volume | channel-0 nucleus voxels inside the cell |

: Metrics. {#tbl-metrics}

**Starriness.** Let $\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i$ be the unit vector from the base to the tip of dendrite $i$ (cells with at
least 3 dendrites). Let $t_1 \ge t_2 \ge t_3$ be the eigenvalues of the orientation tensor
$T = \frac{1}{N_d}\sum_i \hat{\mathbf{u}}_i \hat{\mathbf{u}}_i^{\top}$. Then $s = 0$ when all dendrites lie along one
axis, and $s = 1$ when they spread in a plane or in 3D.

## Do the tags show up in the measurements?

### Feature by feature

For each metric:

- The **test statistic** is the difference in group means.
- The **p-value** comes from a permutation test that shuffles the tags *within each stack* (10 000 permutations).
- The p-values are corrected for the 16 metrics tested with Holm's method [@holm1979].
- The **effect size** is Cliff's $\delta = P(X_{\text{round}} > X_{\text{elong}}) - P(X_{\text{round}} < X_{\text{elong}})$,
  a rank measure [@cliff1993]. $\delta = 0$ means no shift, and $|\delta| \gtrsim 0.47$ is conventionally a large one
  [@romano2006].

{{< include preliminary/_tests.md >}}

: Round vs elongated, sorted by p-value. Bold: significant after Holm correction. {#tbl-tests}

![Main differences: boxes span the quartiles, whiskers 1.5 × the interquartile range, one dot per cell.
Above each panel: Cliff's δ and Holm-corrected p.](preliminary/boxplots.png){#fig-box}

### Do size and dendrite count alone give two groups?

Round cells are larger and carry more dendrites. Does that make two groups that show up without the tags?
Two checks:

1. **Unsupervised.** Gaussian mixtures with 1–3 components are fitted to log body volume and log dendrite count,
   and compared by BIC [@schwarz1978]. If two populations existed, two components should win.
2. **Supervised.** A logistic regression predicts the tag from each feature set. Each stack is predicted by a model
   trained on the other stacks. Agreement is scored by the area under the ROC curve (AUC).

{{< include preliminary/_separation.md >}}

![Left: body volume and dendrite count of every typed cell, coloured by tag. Curves: the count model below,
averaged over stacks. Right: ROC curves of the tag predictions, leaving one stack out.](preliminary/size_dendrites.png){#fig-size}

**Size and dendrite count do not give two groups.** BIC favours a single component, with or without the axis
ratio, and the two-component solution matches the tags only weakly (ARI ≈ 0.2–0.3). The two groups overlap
heavily in @fig-size. Round cells are shifted towards larger size and more dendrites, a continuous shift rather
than a separate population.

The tags are still clearly *reflected* in the numbers:

- Size and dendrite count alone recover them with AUC ≈ 0.76.
- Shape alone does about as well.
- Combining size, dendrites and shape reaches AUC ≈ 0.85.

### More dendrites, or just bigger cells?

Round cells are bigger, and bigger cells have more dendrites, so the higher count could be a size effect.
Two direct comparisons hold size fixed:

- **By size class.** The typed cells are split into four equal-sized classes of body volume, and the two groups
  are compared inside each class.
- **Size-matched cells.** Each round cell is set against the elongated cells *of the same stack* whose body
  volume is within ±25% of its own.

![Left: dendrite count in each body-volume class; bars are medians, n below. Right: each round cell (vertical)
against the mean of its size-matched elongated cells (horizontal). Points above the diagonal are round cells with
more dendrites than elongated cells of the same size and stack.](preliminary/dendrites_by_size.png){#fig-dendrites}

{{< include preliminary/_dendrites.md >}}

What the plots show:

- **Small cells (below about 700 µm³): no difference.** Round and elongated cells carry the same number of
  dendrites. Very few small cells were tagged round.
- **Larger cells: round ones tend to have a few more.** The medians differ by 2–5 dendrites, and most size-matched
  round cells lie above the diagonal.
- **The groups overlap throughout.** In the largest class, much of the difference comes from about six round cells
  with 16–22 dendrites, while the rest overlap the elongated ones. Large cells are also where merged cells,
  segmentation leftovers and the annotator seeing many dendrites are most likely to play a part.

## Connected cells

How many cells are in contact with others, through their processes or bodies? This is measured directly on the label volumes:

- **Gap.** For every pair of cells less than 4 µm apart, the gap is the free space between their masks: $d_{\min} - 1$ voxels,
  with $d_{\min}$ the shortest distance between a voxel of one and a voxel of the other. Masks whose faces touch have gap 0.
- **Link.** Two cells are *linked* if their gap is at most 1.5 µm (about 3 voxels). The tolerance allows for thin
  canaliculi broken by thresholding, the erosion step or partial-volume effects.
- **Groups.** Groups are chains of linked cells.
- **Where they meet.** Each side of a contact lies either in the cell's body (the opening used for the dendrites) or
  in a process.

{{< include preliminary/_connectivity.md >}}

![Left: gaps between all pairs of neighbouring cells (orange: the 1.5 µm tolerance). Middle: share of cells linked
to another, as the tolerance varies. Right: linked neighbours per cell, by tag (bars: medians).](preliminary/connectivity.png){#fig-connectivity}

**How to read this.** The watershed splits continuous dye between the nuclei. Two cells therefore touch whenever the
dye is continuous between them at the stack's threshold, and the contact surface is where the watershed drew the
boundary. A link means continuous or nearly continuous dye. It does not prove that two processes join, but almost
all links are between processes, not merged bodies.

- **Most cells are linked.** About 80% of kept cells belong to a group, and the share hardly depends on the
  tolerance: from about 70% requiring contact to under 90% at 4 µm.
- **Stack 3.2 is the exception.** It has the most isolated cells and the highest foreground threshold. Thresholds
  differ between stacks, so compare numbers within a stack.
- **Links through excluded cells are not seen.** These include junk, rejected regions, soft tissue and the stack
  edges.
- **Round cells have somewhat more linked neighbours.** This is expected given their larger size and dendrite count.

### Groups in 3D

Every group with at least 5 cells is shown below. Each cell is shaded by its tag (blues elongated, oranges round,
greys untyped), with the shade alternating so that neighbours stay distinct. Black spheres mark contacts and grey
spheres near-contacts. Drag to rotate and scroll to zoom. The meshes are simplified for the web.

## Main conclusions (preliminary)

- **Round and elongated cells have the same length.** Body length $a_1 \approx 28$ µm in both groups. "Round" cells
  are *wider and especially thicker*: body thickness is about 9 µm against 6 µm. "Round" therefore means a fuller
  cross-section, not a shorter cell.
- **Round cells are larger.** Body volume is about 2× higher in medians, and about 1.4× after stack effects. This
  follows largely from the thicker cross-section at equal length.
- **Round cells have more dendrites** (median 10 vs 6), mostly because they are bigger. At equal size the
  difference vanishes for small cells. Among larger cells, round ones tend to have a few more (@fig-dendrites), but
  this rests on a handful of very branched cells: it is suggestive, not established. Dendrite *length* (reach,
  process fraction) and *arrangement* (starriness) do not differ.
- **No discrete phenotypes.** Size and dendrite count give one continuous population with the round cells shifted
  within it, not two clusters. The manual tags capture a real gradient: they are recovered with AUC ≈ 0.85, well
  above chance and short of perfect.
- **Nucleus volume and solidity do not differ.**
- **Most cells are connected to neighbours.** About 80% of kept cells are linked to at least one other, almost always
  process to process. Groups contain up to 23 cells, so the segmented cells form networks rather than isolated units.

## Caveats

- **One annotator**, with borderline calls. Inter-rater agreement is not yet measured. Shape differences are partly
  circular, because the tags were given by looking at shape. The size and dendrite results are less so, but
  dendrites are visible in the images used for tagging.
- **Cells are nested in stacks, and stacks in bone samples.** The within-stack permutation removes stack-level
  differences but treats cells in a stack as independent. Stacks 1.1–1.4 come from the same bone sample, so the effective number of independent samples is about 4. A mixed model
  with sample as a random effect is the natural next step once more samples are imaged.
- **Segmentation parameters differ between stacks.** Absolute volumes and counts are not comparable across
  stacks. This is a further reason to compare within stacks.
- **Cells near the stack edges or soft tissue were filtered out**, and dendrites beyond the dye penetration are
  missed. Counts are lower bounds.
